title: Napoleon (2023) might be the most underrated film of year past.

commenti.body: Glad you liked it. To me it felt beyond drive-by in its story and its depiction of Napoleon. Imprecise, zero reason to care about anything. Maybe if it was a mini-series or multiple movies I would’ve liked it more.
[removed]
[removed]

You spend half your write up on the technical elements, and I completely agree that those are fantastic; I listened to the score a ton while reading about him before seeing the film. I still find it to be horrifically disappointing. 

Massive pieces of Bonaparte’s life are skipped over that aren’t just needed as a history nerd, they’re needed for pacing I think. Bonaparte goes from junior officer at Toulon to First Consul in what feels like no time at all, and we still know nothing about him; never mind the bizarre, sniveling portrayal by Phoenix. I could see what you talk about, a realistic grounding of the emperor, being great but this wasn’t it. I think the movie is horrifically tonally imbalanced as well, scenes that should be serious are played for laughs too often, notably Moscow, Egypt, etc. where he’s acting like a petulant child in front of his peers/marshals. Bizarre movie but I’m glad you could enjoy it.

The pacing is definitely one of the movie's shortcomings.

Perhaps the 4-hour director cut will fix that. Fingers crossed!

This movie is shit in silk stockings and is nothing more than 3 hours of character assassination. Scott clearly has no appreciation for the complexity of his legacy and character. The battle scenes are well done, but we're never given any context to them. They're only there for eye candy. In the domestic scenes, he's portrayed as someone in a will Farrel movie. One of the worst films I've seen in theaters, and I've seen Crash and cannibal Holocaust
Exactly. I had fun watching it but I feel it tried to tell way too much in too little time. When the runtime was unveiled, I was like "yikes, that's a bit short."

I’m so curious how this film changed from its inception to the release. I can’t imagine the movie was pitched as a satirical take-down of Napoleon, but large parts of the movie steered hard into that direction, so it makes me wonder when those elements were introduced and whose idea they were. 

My guess is that Joaquin Phoenix came up with this juvenile, absurd take on the character and refused to play it any other way which totally shaped the tone of the film. Had Phoenix not been cast I wonder if the film would have played it more straight and been a standard Scott war epic. In the end I got the “whiplash” you mentioned when it pivoted hard between these two tonally distinct movies. 

Personally, I’d rather see a fully satirical version of it with Phoenix being completely unrestrained. It would probably be a shit-show but I have a feeling it would at least be a lot more memorable than the half-assed satire meets half-assed historical epic movie that we got.

I loved it, but not for the technical elements, which didn't really stand out for me. I loved that it was such a unique take on a story and a genre that I hadn't really seen before. 

It was unfortunately badly marketed as a standard epic movie, with lots of battle shots and cannons and hero poses. But it quickly became apparent that this was exactly the opposite of what the film was going for. It wasn't an epic, it was an anti-epic. After the initial confusion and necessary changing of my expectations I left the cinema very impressed. I'm looking forward to watching it again, without the initial lack of comprehension. I think now I know what it is, I'll be able to enjoy it properly on its own terms.

I loved that it portrayed Napoleon (and everyone else) without the rose-tinted glasses of hagiography that prevent people from seeing him as a real human, but only as a "Great Man", from the outdated concepts of Whig history. It is teue that he was crude, unmannered, ill-educated, scared, panicky, confused, lucky, horny, selfish, pompous, and often out of his depth. Yet this coarse-mannered Corsican hill-bandit still brought Europe to its knees for twenty years. I thought it was an excellent character study. 

I had gone in initially hoping for a standard modern-day blockbuster epic covering the legend's entire career, with all the famous battles and speeches. But someone else will have to make that film, Scott clearly had no interest in that (and I find it somewhat irritating to read negative reviews criticising it for failing to be a different film than what it set out to be). What Scott wanted to film was an original take, an anti-epic, and he succeeded with a crude and frenzied style that I greatly enjoyed.

"scared shitless punk on the battlefield"

Is this how the movie portrays him?

Because it's utter bullshit. He had some 22 horses shot out from under him. Saw one of his Marshals get his head blown off by a cannonball right next to him and didn't flinch, and scouted the perimeter of Waterloo the night before battle with 200 feet of his enemy.

Oddly enough, he was queasy looking at medical models of his stomach when he was ill on St. Helena.
Amen. It is a piece of shit.
This was a huge disappointment for me. Can't understand how they were able to fuck a Napoleon movie that bad. Could easily been an instant classic epic. Sadly the epicness wasn't the main focus...

The British have a long history of poking fun at N and this movie seems to carry on in that tradition.  Scott could have cast 'Maximus' as N but instead chose 'Commodus' which before even seeing the film had to give you a clue as to how it would be treated.  

I can see why people were let down by this and a 'Maximus' style N would have been great but it was entirely intentional and the movie is basically a giant troll on anyone who expected otherwise.  I think its completely self aware to the fact that it would rub a lot of people the wrong way but Scott seemed to enjoy doing just that.  

Once you recalibrate your expectations from epic badass war film to British N satire the movie makes a lot more sense

I had the opposite of a good time watching it. I thought it was put together very poorly. Ridley should've made up his mind about what he wanted to focus on - was it the love story, the battle skills, or the later years? By trying to cover everything, it just came off as a half-baked effort, and we didn't get a real deep dive into any of those aspects (especially the troubled love story!). It's a shame because Joaquin Phoenix delivered another fantastic performance, but it felt like a missed chance.

I felt like it was more of a romantic comedy with some good serious drama. Phoenix played it very comedically and the heart of the movie was his love of Josephine. That dominated the whole movie and for that I really enjoyed it. Like you said , expected something different but loved what I got, and someone else will have to make the serious version.             Also it was close enough to accurate for me.  I never good the vibe he was cowardly on a battle field, more so just the movie portraying the intensity. And the fact is, if you wanna tell a story about Napoleon it has to be about Josephine, she dominated his life, he was madly in love with her, thats real. And they did a good job with that I think
Damn, is my heart warmed reading this. Yes, the film could very easily be read as an anti-epic. I think Scarpa and Scott's deconstruction of Napoleon was very well done.

>Is this how the movie portrays him?

At the very least during Toulon. The fear is mostly gone during indirect combat like Austerlitz or Egypt, and the glimpse of Borodino we're shown presents him as quite fearless, but he is silently TERRIFIED during the battle of Waterloo.

Character assassination? I must object. While I believe it is not without reason that people want their biopics to be historically accurate, it is not that genre's job to be 100% accurate. Narrative cinema is inherently dramatized and sensationalist. Even Oppenheimer wasn't without its spice, namely, the entirely fabricated Einstein pond thing that more or less set Lewis Strauss on Oppie.
Nah, Ridley Scott's responses to criticism feel way too direct for that vision not to be his.

Everyone complaining it wasn't a perfectly detailed historical pseudo-documentary needs to touch grass. 


Can't recognize art and technical achievement by an extremely gifted filmmaker when it smacks them in the senses. 


It was an ambitious, daring, and even quite experimental, big budget Hollywood film.


Hollywood is dying and needs that sort of creative juice and yet so called 'film lovers' are pissed it didn't play out like a Wiki article lmao
Don't even bother, man, these people youre replying to don't get the film at all.
There is a 4 hour version coming to Apple+ in March.
I’m curious about it but still don’t think it’ll fix some of the fatal flaws with the story/characterizations

Why would he be terrified at Toulon when it was his fucking idea in the first place?

Fuck everything about that director
